Executive Summary for Extreme Heat and Fire Risk Across Spain
Spain’s weather outlook for 7 September 2026 points to a sharp contrast between a wet, cloudy Cantabrian north and a hot, dry south and interior under strong high-pressure influence. Orange-level warnings for extreme heat are in force across the southern Andalusian countryside, including areas of Cordoba, Seville and Jaen, where highs of up to 40°C are forecast, while a wider band of yellow warnings covers Extremadura, Madrid, Castilla-La Mancha, interior Valencia and Alicante, Murcia, Aragon and parts of Catalonia and the Balearic Islands, with highs between 34°C and 39°C. An additional orange alert applies to eastern, southern and western Gran Canaria for sustained heat with tropical nights, alongside a separate yellow coastal-wind warning for the western Canary Islands. Prolonged high temperatures and dry conditions over these interior and southern areas are typically associated with elevated wildfire risk during this period of the year.
- Date of Event: 07 September 2026
- Location: Andalusia (Cordoba, Seville, Jaen), Extremadura, Madrid, Castilla-La Mancha, interior Valencia and Alicante, Region of Murcia, Aragon, Lleida (Catalonia), Balearic Islands and the Canary Islands, Spain
- Risk Category: Environment
What is Risk Analysis in the Context of Environment Events
Environmental risk analysis assesses the impact of extreme heat warnings on public health, outdoor activity and wildfire potential. When high pressure locks dry, hot air over a region for an extended period, daytime temperatures climb sharply, overnight cooling is limited in warning-level zones, and dry vegetation becomes more susceptible to ignition, all of which raise the burden on health services, outdoor workers and, in the driest interior and southern areas, the wildfire risk profile.
Known Hotspots and Sensitive Areas
High Impact
- Seville and the Guadalquivir valley, under an orange warning with highs forecast to reach 40°C
- Cordoba and the Cordoba and Seville countryside (campina), under an orange warning with highs around 39°C
- Jaen, including the Morena and Condado districts and the Guadalquivir valley, under an orange warning for extreme heat
- Eastern, southern and western Gran Canaria, under an orange warning for heat with tropical nights near 26°C
Medium Impact
- Extremadura, with Caceres reaching around 37°C and Badajoz around 38°C under yellow warnings
- Madrid, Castilla-La Mancha (Toledo, Ciudad Real, Cuenca, Albacete) and the Region of Murcia, with highs of 36°C to 38°C under yellow warnings
- Interior Valencia and Alicante, Aragon (Zaragoza, Lleida) and parts of the Balearic Islands, including the south and interior of Mallorca, with highs of 34°C to 38°C under yellow warnings
Low Impact
- The Cantabrian coast and Galicia’s Atlantic seaboard, where cloud and Atlantic humidity keep highs in the low-to-mid 20s°C
- Mediterranean coastal cities such as Malaga and Almeria, where sea breezes hold highs closer to 27-28°C
- Western Canary Islands (Tenerife, La Gomera, El Hierro), affected mainly by a separate yellow coastal-wind warning rather than the extreme-heat alerts
Impact on Transportation and Services
A yellow warning for coastal phenomena is in force for Gran Canaria, Tenerife, La Gomera and El Hierro, with north to northeast winds of 50 to 61 km/h forecast, which is expected to affect maritime navigation and inter-island ferry channels. On the mainland, sustained high temperatures in interior and southern provinces raise the operational burden on outdoor services and can prompt local authorities to restrict agricultural burning and outdoor works during peak afternoon hours in the highest-risk districts.

The meteorological start of autumn has already passed. And yet, the Canary Islands are set to experience another spell of high summer weather. The archipelago is kicking off the week with temperatures of up to 37 degrees. It is set to remain hot until at least Wednesday.
Temperatures of over 30 degrees were already being recorded in the early hours of Monday morning. For example, Agüimes on Gran Canaria recorded 30.7 degrees shortly after four o’clock. It cannot be a case of a single faulty thermometer, as just a few minutes later the temperature in San Bartolomé de Tirajana was 29.5 degrees. Other stations belonging to the state meteorological service AEMET in the Canary Islands also recorded similar figures.
The highest temperatures were therefore all recorded in Gran Canaria. Parts of the island are the only region in the Canary Islands to be placed on an orange alert. And it’s set to get hot elsewhere too:
The Canary Islands are expecting midsummer weather at the start of autumn
The AEMET issued no fewer than four heat warnings for the Canary Islands from 10.00 am on Monday. At the start of the week, the heat is sweeping across the Canary Islands from the east. Lanzarote and Fuerteventura are expecting temperatures of up to 34 degrees Celsius. In the south of Tenerife, temperatures will reach up to 34. Gran Canaria is expected to see up to 36 degrees in the higher elevations and, in the south, the weekly record of 37 degrees.
Heat warnings are already in place for all the islands as early as Tuesday : the AEMET is forecasting temperatures of up to 38 degrees in the south, west and east of Gran Canaria. Temperatures of up to 36 degrees are expected in Lanzarote and in the south, west and east of Tenerife. The other forecasts remain unchanged. However, La Gomera, La Palma and El Hierro will be added to the list, with temperatures there also reaching up to 36 degrees. The north-west of Tenerife is expected to reach 34 degrees.
The intense heat is expected to fall back below the threshold for widespread warnings as early as Wednesday. Gran Canaria will remain the only island under a weather warning, with temperatures still expected to reach 34 in the south, west and east. The rest of the archipelago can still expect high summer temperatures. According to AEMET, Fuerteventura will still reach up to 33 degrees, Tenerife up to 32 and the western islands up to 29 degrees.

TAGBILARAN CITY — The Visayas power grid was placed under Red Alert from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. on Monday, Sept. 7, as available power supply fell short of projected electricity demand, according to the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP).
The grid was placed under Yellow Alert from noon to 1 p.m. and from 8 p.m. to 9 p.m.
As of 1:30 p.m., the Visayas grid had an available capacity of 2,284 megawatts (MW) against a demand of 2,470 MW, leaving a supply shortfall of 186 MW.
NGCP said 11 power plants were on forced outage, while 15 plants were operating at derated capacities, resulting in a total of 919 MW of generating capacity unavailable to the grid.
Of the plants on forced outage, five had been unavailable since August, one since July, two since June, seven since May, three since 2025, two since 2024, two since 2023, and one since 2021.
NGCP identified the unavailability of the Visayas’ large coal-fired power plants, Therma Visayas Inc. (THVI) 1 and Panay Energy Development Corporation 3, as one of the major factors behind the Red and Yellow Alert declarations.
The generating capacity of THVI 2 was also reduced by 70 MW because of a main steam problem, further limiting the supply available to the grid.
Article continues after this advertisement
Another factor was the limited power import from Mindanao, which NGCP said was due to an increase in the demand forecast in Mindanao.
The Red Alert declaration means the power system is operating with insufficient reserve capacity to meet demand and contingencies, raising the possibility of power interruptions if the supply situation worsens.

Korea to Unveil Additional Chuseok Price Relief Measures This Week
Discounts on Farm and Fishery Goods, Expanded Seafood Supply
Larger Supply of Holiday Staples and Discount Support
Additional Livelihood Stabilization Package Due This Week
"Grocery Prices Are the Economic Team's Report Card"
Lee Hyoung-il, the nominee for deputy prime minister for economy and minister of economy and finance, said on the 7th that the government will finalize and announce supplementary measures to its Chuseok livelihood stabilization package this week, including discounts on agricultural, livestock and fishery products and an expanded seafood supply.
Lee, who currently serves as first vice minister of economy and finance, made the remarks during a visit to Kkachisan Market, a traditional market in Seoul's Gangseo District, where he reviewed supply and demand trends for holiday staples and the progress of the Chuseok package. He checked prices of vegetables and fruits, as well as six popular fish species including mackerel and pollock, of which 20,000 tons from government reserves have been released at discounts of up to 40% below market prices. "We will do our utmost to ease the burden of grocery prices through an expanded supply of holiday staples and discount support," he said.
Price stability is a task Lee has emphasized repeatedly as concerns mount over rising prices of holiday staples and farm, livestock and fishery products ahead of Chuseok. At his first press briefing on the 2nd of this month, he said grocery prices in people's daily lives are the economic team's report card.
President Lee Jae-myung also pressed the nominee to focus on stabilizing prices of holiday staples when he received a report on the Chuseok package at a recent Cabinet meeting. "Everyone complains that prices go up when Chuseok comes around. Are you confident this time? I could withdraw the nomination for finance minister, so is this really certain?" the president said in a pointed joke.
Lee also held a meeting with small business owners at the Korea Federation of Micro Enterprise's digital education center in Seoul's Mapo District on the same day. "Stabilizing the operations of small business owners and supporting their growth are important to easing polarization in our economy," he said. "We will make every policy effort to ensure the warmth of growth reaches all small business owners."
